question.problem:
Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-5, & x\le -1 \\ 2ax+3b, & -1<x\le 2 \\ 4, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
At $x=-1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & =f(-1) \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(-1)+3b \\  & =-2a+3b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) \\ -5 & =-2a+3b \\ 2a-3b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, at $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(2)+3b \\  & =4a+3b,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}4=4.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ 4a+3b & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve the following system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2a-3b=5 \\ 4a+3b=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding both equations we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6a & =9 \\ a & =\frac{9}{6} \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can replace $a$ by $\frac{3}{2}$ into the first equation. Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(\frac{3}{2})-3b & =5 \\ 3-3b & =5 \\ -3b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2$ for $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\frac{2}{3}.$
